scenes.tts: Archaea moved because a repeated pattern challenged one old group. How do we decide whether another branch should move? Start with the current tree as a claim. Then ask which relationship each new comparison supports.
scenes.caption: Archaea moved because a repeated pattern challenged one old group. How do we decide whether another branch should move? Start with the current tree as a claim. Then ask which relationship each new comparison supports.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's tree and exact COLOR MAP: Archaea teal, Bacteria blue, Eukarya gold, evidence white. Keep a small 'schematic' label on screen throughout. Zoom into the gold Eukarya branch. Attach a white tag reading 'current claim' to its branch joint.
scenes.narration: Archaea moved because a repeated pattern challenged one old group. How do we decide whether another branch should move? Start with the current tree as a claim. Then ask which relationship each new comparison supports.

scenes.visual: Keep the gold branch swaying gently. Write 'When Evidence Redraws a Branch', then transform the title into an evidence-card tray beside the tree.

scenes.tts: Fungi once seemed plant-like because they grow in place and have cell walls. On our tree, a mushroom icon begins beside a plant. That placement is a hypothesis about ancestry. Looking alike can suggest a group, but the branch must survive other tests.
scenes.caption: Fungi once seemed plant-like because they grow in place and have cell walls. On our tree, a mushroom icon begins beside a plant. That placement is a hypothesis about ancestry. Looking alike can suggest a group, but the branch must survive other tests.
scenes.visual: Inside the gold branch, enlarge a schematic plant, mushroom and animal. The mushroom rests beside the plant under a white card labelled 'appearance'. Draw a dotted branch joint labelled 'hypothesis', never 'wrong'. Leaves and mushroom cap move gently.
scenes.narration: Fungi once seemed plant-like because they grow in place and have cell walls. On our tree, a mushroom icon begins beside a plant. That placement is a hypothesis about ancestry. Looking alike can suggest a group, but the branch must survive other tests.

scenes.tts: Protein comparisons supplied another test. Several protein trees grouped the sampled fungi with animals. Shared added or missing stretches supported the same relationship. The mushroom branch slides beside the animal branch. This does not mean animals came from modern mushrooms.
scenes.caption: Protein comparisons supplied another test. Several protein trees grouped the sampled fungi with animals. Shared added or missing stretches supported the same relationship. The mushroom branch slides beside the animal branch. This does not mean animals came from modern mushrooms.
scenes.visual: A white 'protein comparisons' card unfolds into aligned labelled blocks, not molecular structures. Matching gap markers glow on mushroom and animal rows. Their branch tips pivot together while the plant stays put. Add 'shared ancestor' over the new joint.
scenes.narration: Protein comparisons supplied another test. Several protein trees grouped the sampled fungi with animals. Shared added or missing stretches supported the same relationship. The mushroom branch slides beside the animal branch. This does not mean animals came from modern mushrooms.

scenes.tts: A result can be a clue, not a final verdict. Confidence grows when different comparisons support the same branch and sampling is broad enough. Conflicting results send scientists back to methods, markers and organisms. The tree stays open to testing.
scenes.caption: A result can be a clue, not a final verdict. Confidence grows when different comparisons support the same branch and sampling is broad enough. Conflicting results send scientists back to methods, markers and organisms. The tree stays open to testing.
scenes.visual: Three white evidence cards push gently on the fungus-animal joint. Two align; one points elsewhere and becomes a question card. The joint steadies but remains drawn with a small hinge. Labels 'methods', 'markers' and 'samples' circle the question.
scenes.narration: A result can be a clue, not a final verdict. Confidence grows when different comparisons support the same branch and sampling is broad enough. Conflicting results send scientists back to methods, markers and organisms. The tree stays open to testing.

scenes.tts: A new evidence card supports the branch already drawn, and no strong comparison challenges it. Should scientists move that branch, keep it, or erase the whole tree? Choose before the card reaches the joint.
scenes.caption: A new evidence card supports the branch already drawn, and no strong comparison challenges it. Should scientists move that branch, keep it, or erase the whole tree? Choose before the card reaches the joint.
scenes.visual: Show one schematic branch and a moving white card whose arrow matches that joint. Place three large choices around it: 'move', 'keep', 'erase all'. The card travels slowly toward the branch without touching.
scenes.narration: A new evidence card supports the branch already drawn, and no strong comparison challenges it. Should scientists move that branch, keep it, or erase the whole tree? Choose before the card reaches the joint.

scenes.visual: Hold the three choices and question. The evidence card continues a slow orbit around the unchanged branch. A thin progress arc sweeps once.

scenes.tts: Keep it. New evidence does not require movement. It may strengthen the present relationship instead. Revision belongs where the evidence changes the picture. Scientists should not rebuild every branch because a well-supported branch was tested.
scenes.caption: Keep it. New evidence does not require movement. It may strengthen the present relationship instead. Revision belongs where the evidence changes the picture. Scientists should not rebuild every branch because a well-supported branch was tested.
scenes.visual: The card clicks beside the existing joint and brightens it. The 'move' and 'erase all' choices drift away without red crosses. Zoom back to show untouched teal, blue and other gold branches continuing their ambient motion.
scenes.narration: Keep it. New evidence does not require movement. It may strengthen the present relationship instead. Revision belongs where the evidence changes the picture. Scientists should not rebuild every branch because a well-supported branch was tested.

scenes.tts: The same logic reaches species. Nuclear DNA supported treating forest and savanna elephants as separate species. Yet one large study sampled very few animals of each kind. Broad stretches of DNA strengthened the split, while the small sample kept a limit visible.
scenes.caption: The same logic reaches species. Nuclear DNA supported treating forest and savanna elephants as separate species. Yet one large study sampled very few animals of each kind. Broad stretches of DNA strengthened the split, while the small sample kept a limit visible.
scenes.visual: Transform the gold subtree into two schematic elephant silhouettes, one forest and one savanna. Many tiny white genome-location blocks fill a wide bar. Only a few sample tokens sit below it. Keep a large 'small sample' tag beside the supported split.
scenes.narration: The same logic reaches species. Nuclear DNA supported treating forest and savanna elephants as separate species. Yet one large study sampled very few animals of each kind. Broad stretches of DNA strengthened the split, while the small sample kept a limit visible.

scenes.tts: DNA comparisons also placed whales among even-toed hoofed mammals, with hippos as their closest living relatives. Gene sequences split the old Protista kingdom into many branches. These changes differ in scale, but each asks which tree fits the evidence. Each change still needs its own evidence and its own limits.

scenes.visual: Transform the elephant split into a gold whale-and-hippo joint, then into several gold protist branches marked 'schematic'. Keep white DNA and gene-sequence cards driving each transformation. A small white 'limits' tag rides beside each changed branch.

scenes.tts: Reclassification changes the scientific model. It does not make organisms switch ancestors, and it does not prove earlier scientists careless. They used the evidence available. Better tools can reveal patterns that shape, habitat or a short comparison could not show.
scenes.caption: Reclassification changes the scientific model. It does not make organisms switch ancestors, and it does not prove earlier scientists careless. They used the evidence available. Better tools can reveal patterns that shape, habitat or a short comparison could not show.
scenes.visual: Return to the full shared-colour tree. The organism icons remain fixed while only labelled branch lines redraw around them. An older evidence tray and a newer evidence tray appear in sequence. Neither receives a blame symbol.
scenes.narration: Reclassification changes the scientific model. It does not make organisms switch ancestors, and it does not prove earlier scientists careless. They used the evidence available. Better tools can reveal patterns that shape, habitat or a short comparison could not show.

scenes.tts: Ask these questions whenever a group changes. What relationship did the old tree claim? What new pattern challenges it? What important limits remain? Those questions turn a changed label into a clear evidence-based scientific explanation.
scenes.caption: Ask these questions whenever a group changes. What relationship did the old tree claim? What new pattern challenges it? What important limits remain? Those questions turn a changed label into a clear evidence-based scientific explanation.
scenes.visual: Three white question cards orbit the central tree in order: 'old claim?', 'new pattern?', 'limits?'. Each locks beside the appropriate branch joint. The tree fills most of the frame and continues to move.
